**Section IV: Essay (10 marks).** Write an essay of between 250 and 300 words on any one of the following topics.

**Topic 1.** You have been asked by the editor of your school journal to write an article about some facts and myths about AIDS. Write the article, making sure that you choose examples from the daily life experiences of your fellow students. Remember that your parents will read the article.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
La rédaction anglaise du BAC sanctionne autant le respect du format imposé (article de journal scolaire, discours devant un public de parents, lettre personnelle à un correspondant étranger) que le contenu. Un article informatif doit rester factuel et accessible à un lectorat mixte (élèves et parents) ; un discours devant des parents doit à la fois reconnaître une part de responsabilité et exposer un point de vue, sur un ton respectueux mais ferme ; une lettre personnelle à un correspondant garde un registre amical tout en corrigeant des idées reçues avec tact plutôt qu'avec agressivité. Comme le sujet propose un choix, un seul texte doit être rédigé le jour de l'examen ; les trois modèles ci-dessous illustrent chacun l'un des formats possibles.

## Topic 1 - School journal article (modèle, environ 270 mots)

**Facts and Myths About AIDS: What You Really Need to Know**

Many students in our school still believe things about AIDS that are simply not true, and some of these myths can be dangerous. It is time we separated fact from rumour.

**Myth: You can catch AIDS by sharing a meal or shaking hands with someone who is infected.** This is false. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, is transmitted mainly through unprotected sexual contact, contaminated blood, or from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy or breastfeeding. It does not spread through ordinary daily contact such as sharing food, hugging, or sitting next to someone in class.

**Myth: Only certain kinds of people get AIDS.** Many students assume AIDS only affects people who behave "badly." In reality, anyone who has unprotected sex or comes into contact with infected blood, regardless of their background, can be infected. Judging people based on this myth only isolates those who are already struggling.

**Fact: Prevention is possible and effective.** Using protection during sexual activity, avoiding the sharing of sharp objects such as razors, and getting tested when in doubt are simple, effective ways to protect ourselves and others.

**Fact: A person living with HIV can live a long, active life.** Thanks to modern treatment, HIV is no longer the automatic death sentence many of us imagine; people who receive proper care can live for decades.

I hope that by reading this article, some of you will think twice before repeating myths that have circulated in our school for years. Understanding AIDS correctly is the first step towards protecting ourselves and treating those affected with the respect they deserve.

**Section IV: Essay (10 marks).** Write an essay of between 250 and 300 words on any one of the following topics.

**Topic 2.** Imagine that the President of the Parent Teachers' Association invites you in your college. This is because the teachers have complained that the older boys and girls in the school are setting a bad example to the younger ones. Write your speech to the parents in which you will accept some blame for what is going on but at the same time you may want to explain that young people are not understood.
questions.corrige_markdown:
## Topic 2 - Speech to parents (modèle, environ 260 mots)

Dear parents,

I want to thank you for inviting me to speak today, even though I know the reason is not a happy one: the concern that some of us, the older students, have been setting a bad example for the younger ones.

I will not stand here and deny that this concern is fair. Some of us have indeed behaved in ways we should not have, forgetting that younger students look up to us more than we sometimes realise. For that, on behalf of those of us who have acted carelessly, I want to say we are sorry, and we understand why it worries you.

But I also want to ask you, respectfully, to understand something from our side. Growing up today is not always easy to understand from the outside. We face pressures that did not exist in the same way when many of you were our age: pressure to fit in, pressure from what we see online, and sometimes very little space to make mistakes without being immediately judged as "bad examples" rather than young people still learning.

I am not asking you to excuse poor behaviour. I am asking that, alongside holding us accountable, you also try to talk with us rather than only about us, so that the younger students see not just our mistakes being punished, but also adults and older students working together to correct them.

If we manage that together, I believe the good example everyone wants for the younger ones will follow naturally, built on understanding rather than fear alone.

Thank you for listening.

**Section IV: Essay (10 marks).** Write an essay of between 250 and 300 words on any one of the following topics.

**Topic 3.** You have a pen friend in England and she has written to you about some of the things that she has heard about Africa. Many of the ideas are wrong. Write a letter in which you try to correct some of the mistaken ideas about Africa. In the letter your name must be Marcel Nang and you are a student in Lycée d'Abong Mbang.
questions.corrige_markdown:
## Topic 3 - Personal letter (modèle, environ 250 mots)

Dear Sarah,

Thank you for your last letter. I noticed that some of the things you mentioned hearing about Africa are not quite accurate, so I wanted to write back and clear a few things up, as your friend from Lycée d'Abong Mbang.

First, you mentioned imagining Africa as one single place where everyone lives the same way. In reality, Africa is a huge continent with over fifty countries, thousands of languages, and enormous differences between one region and another. My own country, Cameroon, is sometimes called "Africa in miniature" precisely because it already contains such a variety of landscapes and cultures within its own borders.

You also asked whether most people here still live in villages without electricity or schools. While rural life is certainly part of our reality, many of us live in cities with universities, hospitals, shopping centres and internet access, much like anywhere else. I am writing to you from a computer at school, after all.

Finally, you mentioned being surprised that African students study subjects like literature, mathematics and philosophy "just like in Europe." I understand why this might surprise someone who has only seen certain images of Africa in the media, but our school system is demanding, and many of my classmates hope to study at university, in Cameroon or abroad, just as you do.

I hope this helps give you a slightly different picture of where I live. Write back soon and tell me more about your own daily life in England too.

Your friend,
Marcel Nang
